Hello my friends

Let me first apologize for continuing to test your patience with an endless barrage of "using film for the first time" questions, but no matter how much is said on the subject, the question that is core to my current anxieties remains unvoiced:

What's the flattest glass an average guy can obtain for sandwiching holographic film during exposure?

An answer I may hear: Old plates - Yeah, they are made from exceptionally flat glass, but I don't have any old plates large enough.

And because the instinctive reaction to flexible film questions seems to be "Use plates instead, dude", I will explain why this is not a viable option:

A. Too expensive. 'Nuff said.

B. My latest endeavor involves mechanized slit mask translation across the face of the film. Yep - I'm giving stereograms a shot. Yes, this is a monumentally ambitious undertaking for a beginner holographer - noted - but it's what I'm doing. Heck, why not join the Olympic hurdle team after only a few toddling, uncertain steps?

Anyway... A pair of lead screws will be sliding a cardstock slit up the film, and I can't abide by having a delicate layer of emulsion exposed to this harassment. I will therefore be using film sandwiched between over-sized pieces of glass with 7.3 mil tape around the borders and under any clamp points. Index matching is a battle I will save for another day. Today my question is simple:

What's the safest bet for easily-obtained glass for film sandwiches? Will any glazier be in a position to source nice, thick, flatter-than-average glass or should I be prepared to approach a specialty market of some sort?

Many thanks and infinite respect for any insight rendered - and again - apologies for continuing to whack the crap out of this dead horse.

posts.content_md:
No apologies necessary! We are all here to learn holography. Yes for the most flat glass ,will be from old plates, its not necessary to really worry about total flatness for display holography , you can easily find/use plate glass available at your local glazier, art store or roadside trash. You will need to recognize this flatness. The way i do it, is to look at the plate surface and see a reflection of an object far away, now move your head side to side and observe the reflected object. Does the image slide nicely across the plate (especially at edges)? Good glass. Or does it distort wildly? Bad glass. Its easy to see once you know 

what to look for........

posts.content_md:
When I made stereograms, the slit was always in contact with the emulsion. This was to prevent object beam light from fogging the areas adjacent to the slit being exposed, as it expands beyond the slit and through the front glass thickness.

Also, the material used for the slit was a piece of film, exposed and developed to be black, then cut to form slit edges. Craig Newswanger taught me that trick.

Well I am not going to point out things you state you already know so...

You want a low iron glass to keep that "green" from becoming a factor when going thick. Yes thick is better but this will indeed bring your slit away from the emulsion. And as BobH stated you will get areas of overlap neat the edges of the slit. So if you insist on using the sandwich technique, use glass that is "Just thick enough".

Here is a place that sells nice clear glass. I got some from then and have not used it. I may be able to find it stashed away somewhere if you need. You will have to call them for pricing as I forgot what i paid.

[http://www.guardian.com/en/na/gp_001018.html](http://www.guardian.com/en/na/gp_001018.html)

All that said, some ordinary double thick window pane glass will probably do fine for what you want to achieve.

This is a similar post to Justin's other thread about another stereogram machine that I was involved with, that of the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. We were using 16mm film against all conventional wisdom, and got very good images. The controller in that case wasn't even a computer; a bunch of 555 timers and 4017 sequencers! Don't forget we weren't using computer images, just sending a signal to a thrift store movie projector (although outfitted with Canon Camera lenses) to advance to the next frame.

Anyhow the plate holder on this was a photographic contact print frame resized to 30 by 40 cm for film, and the film was squished flat up against a piece of double strength glass from behind with a couple of pieces of spring steel.

Hullo all!

This machine that I've been obsessing over for the last couple of months (which is pure genius, by the by) is essentially designed around a sheet of 10" x 12" glass, so that I can eventually burn 8x10 film, but can initially get it working with 4x5.

My commitment to this design feature is based upon the clever idea I had involving means of jigging my film behind the carriage that will carry the slit mask and getting it right in the dark: The rear piece of glass will have four rare earth magnets epoxied to it - one in each corner. These magnets I found are mounting magnets, with a through hole that is countersunk for screw heads. These countersunk holes will magnetically register to steel set screws protruding from the aluminum structure of the risers. The bottom edge of this anchor glass will rest upon an aluminum deck which will bear the weight, then I'll simply click the magnets back against the set screws (which I can of course adjust so that the glass is plumb to the carriage travel).

And this is why I am s committed to using the sheets of glass. Maybe a thick back sheet with a thinner front sheet and my film in between...

posts.content_md:
A piece of black glass as the backer for your film sandwich will only work as an anti-halation layer if it is index-matched to the film. Otherwise, you'll get reflections off both glass pieces *and* the film.

Another thing you can do instead of index matching is to paint the film base black before exposure. Then, mount it dry and expose. When done, put the film into a tray of water and gently peel the paint layer off the base. It will come off, but you need to be gentle. Then process the film.

Problem with that technique is that you need to spray paint in safelight conditions. And it's messy. And you need to do a bunch of cleaning. I find dealing with index matching fluid much easier.
